extracted.intended_audience: artists, architects, craftsmen, and critics concerned with sculpture, architecture, and stained-glass work
extracted.subtask_description: Guiding principles and standards for designing, executing, and judging architectural sculpture, column/shaft composition, and work in glass (vessels and windows), with ancillary notes on dress and inscription legibility in Venetian context. Emphasises fidelity to material, honesty of structure, and appropriate use of medium-specific effects.

rubrics_metrics.name: Match artistic aims to the material
rubrics_metrics.description: “All art, working with given materials, must propose to itself the objects which, with those materials, are most perfectly attainable; and becomes illegitimate and debased if it propose to itself any other objects, better attainable with other materials.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Choose subjects and effects that the medium can express well; avoid forcing a medium to attempt effects it inherently cannot or can only imperfectly render. Example: intricate fibrous detail suits painting/metalwork, not sculpture. Anti-pattern: carving extreme filamentary detail in marble because it is better achieved in paint or metal.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit sculpture to what the material can easily express
rubrics_metrics.description: Sculpture should not profess as its chief end the expression of great slenderness, lightness, or intricacy (e.g., twigs, bird's nests) which are easily and perfectly expressible in painting and metal-work but only imperfectly in sculpture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When a sculptural subject requires extremely delicate or fibrous structure, represent only the general form and as much detail as can be achieved with ease and honesty in the stone. Example given: carve a bird's nest only as general form plus minimal fibrous suggestion; avoid prolonged labour to simulate filaments.

rubrics_metrics.name: Honor and exhibit the peculiar qualities of the material
rubrics_metrics.description: The workman should set himself to bring out the beauty of the material: if in marble, exhibit transparency and solidity; if in iron, its strength and tenacity; if in gold, its ductility.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design and finish should eulogize the medium’s characteristic virtues so the work is ‘nobler’ for being expressive of its substance. Anti-pattern: treating marble as if it were metal or glass without regard to its visual properties.

rubrics_metrics.name: Glass: emphasize ductility (vessels) and transparency (windows)
rubrics_metrics.description: Glass has two main qualities deserving exhibition — its DUCTILITY when heated, and TRANSPARENCY when cold; in vessels we should exhibit ductility, and in windows transparency.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For blown/moulded glass vessels, celebrate fluid, immediate forms; for windows, prioritize optical purity and light-transmission and use of brilliant color. Anti-patterns: over-refined contours in vessels; turning windows into densely painted opaque pictures.

rubrics_metrics.name: Reject cut glass for dishonoring ductility
rubrics_metrics.description: “All cut glass is barbarous: for the cutting conceals its ductility, and confuses it with crystal.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid cutting and faceting that make glass appear as hard crystal, thereby denying the medium’s malleable, blown character. Preference for forms showing spontaneity of blow/mould rather than chiselled precision.

rubrics_metrics.name: Avoid excessive finish and delicate outlines in glass
rubrics_metrics.description: “All very neat, finished, and perfect form in glass is barbarous: for this fails in proclaiming ... the ease with which its light substance can be moulded or blown.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Favor spontaneous, somewhat irregular, 'fantastic and fickle' grace over minute finish. Encourage wild, extravagant, grotesque yet graceful forms appropriate to rapid execution. Anti-pattern: painstakingly refined glass forms that suggest a different medium.

rubrics_metrics.name: Limit labour on functional glass vessels
rubrics_metrics.description: No workman ought ever to spend more than an hour in the making of any glass vessel.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: For everyday glassware, accept and manifest the material’s fragility and rapid manufacture; avoid expending prolonged labour or 'real art' on articles of daily use. Reserve prolonged precision for appropriate, durable materials.

rubrics_metrics.name: Do not turn stained-glass windows into oil-paint pictures
rubrics_metrics.description: “The attempt to turn painted windows into pretty pictures is one of the most gross and ridiculous barbarisms ...”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid using glass as a direct substitute for oil-paint pictorial technique: it reverses natural light/shadow relations and misuses the material’s qualities. Instead stained glass should be 'serene, intense, brilliant, like flaming jewellery,' with easily legible, quaint subjects and simple, subtle harmonies of color. Historic models: French twelfth- and thirteenth-century windows.

rubrics_metrics.name: Preserve the transparency and sanctity of colored glass in windows
rubrics_metrics.description: Using glass for pictorial opacity denies the transparency that is its 'great spiritual character' and typical expression in church architecture.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design window glass to admit and transform light, using vivid, legible color harmonies rather than opaque painted modelling. Benefit: stained glass as a means of spiritual/architectural expression rather than pictorial simulation.

rubrics_metrics.name: Display shafts to show their material beauty (position near wall)
rubrics_metrics.description: Set pillars/shafts within two or three inches of the wall so they form a 'grove of golden marble' and the wall serves as a relief that brings out the shaft's color and quality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Positioning shafts close to a wall sharpens their shadow and color in sunshine, enhancing visual effect. Anti-pattern: leaving shafts isolated with broad vacant space behind so the eye passes into vacancy and loses appreciation of the shaft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Be honest about the structural role of shafts (expose independence)
rubrics_metrics.description: Leave many shafts visibly with half their capitals projecting beyond the archivolts they sustain, showing that the wall is slightly dependent on them and many are little more than bonds or connecting rods.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Avoid deception that makes minor shafts appear to carry more weight than they do; expose their limited structural role through visible detail. This honesty prevents the appearance of doing more work than allotted to the shaft.

rubrics_metrics.name: Proper superimposition of shafts: diminish and multiply upwards
rubrics_metrics.description: The middle-sized shafts are sorted into two classes; the upper shafts diminish in size and multiply in number so that the lower pillars would balance them safely even without cement — the only right superimposition in the case of shafts.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Design superimposition so upper orders are smaller and more numerous, balancing the lower ones by proportion and count rather than stacking identical shafts. Anticipate critics accustomed to Renaissance stacking (shaft on shaft) who may call this 'against law.'

rubrics_metrics.name: Provide intermediate plinth/tablet for detached marble branches
rubrics_metrics.description: Marble branches, having no vital connexion with the stem, must be provided with a firm tablet or second foundation whereon to stand — an intermediate plinth running along the façade about eighteen inches thick.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: When independent marble shafts or clusters are applied atop other elements, give them visible, substantial bases or tablet foundations to be honest about their support; leave such plinths plainly treated as hard service elements.

rubrics_metrics.name: Sustain porticos with detached clusters balanced on a grand shaft
rubrics_metrics.description: Small porticos are sustained on detached clusters of four or five columns, forming continuation of upper series, each cluster balanced on one grand detached shaft; as much trust being placed in the pillars here as is withdrawn elsewhere.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use one large detached shaft as the real sustaining element under clustered shafts to express balance and poise. Design priorities: balance (poise) rather than breadth of foundation; if poise fails, structure falls.

rubrics_metrics.name: Express importance by altering proportions (thicker and shorter lower shaft)
rubrics_metrics.description: To make an increase of diameter more manifest to the eye, the old builders made the shaft shorter as well as thicker, increasing the depth both of its capital and the base, producing what seems incongruous to the thoughtless but is a 'beautiful expression of constructive genius.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Manipulate relative height, diameter, and capital/base depth to communicate a shaft’s structural importance; visual contrivance (shorter but thicker) can eloquently indicate function and weight distribution.

rubrics_metrics.name: Use base orientation in plan to express intent about balance
rubrics_metrics.description: A circular base sustaining a hexagonal plinth set obliquely to the walls of the church, as if to mark that it did not matter how the base was set, so only that the weights were justly disposed above it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Use plan orientation, obliquity, and variation in plinth geometry to communicate structural ideas (balance, indifferent orientation) to the observer; such choices can convey the builder’s purpose beyond mere utility.

rubrics_metrics.name: Place inscriptions where they are legible to intended viewers
rubrics_metrics.description: Inscriptions written on the soffit of face arches supported by shafts 'could not be read by the congregation, and only with difficulty by those immediately underneath them.'
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Ensure inscriptions are sited and oriented so their text is accessible to the intended audience; illegible placement invites restoration errors and misinterpretation. Note: restorers have introduced wrong letters in inaccessible inscriptions.

rubrics_metrics.name: Dress as a designed civic/ethical expression
rubrics_metrics.description: Venetians 'made their dress a matter of conscience' to show equality, modesty, honour, and to avoid giving offence; a long dress was deliberately chosen to express gravity and peace.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Treat costume as communicative of social values — designers and critics should assess clothing by how well it embodies communal ideals (equality, modesty, temperance) rather than mere fashion or convenience.
